parole.significato: Combining form used to form prefixed perfective verbs with the approximate meanings "to throw" or "to overthrow".
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *vьrgnǫti, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wergʷ-, less likely from *h₂werg-.

parole.significato: Used to form verbs from nouns, adjectives, or foreign verbs.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ovati.

parole.significato: Used to form adjectives from nouns, often relational (meaning "related to X"): -ian, -ic, -ish
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ьskъ, from Proto-Indo-European *-iskos.

parole.significato: suffix appended to nouns and adjectives to create a neuter noun, usually an abstract noun denoting a relation, social s…
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ьstvo.

parole.significato: why!, well I never!, wow! (an exclamation of surprise, especially at an unexpected meeting)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ba.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *běgati, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰegʷ-, cognate with Lithuanian bėgti and Ancient Greek φέβομαι (phébomai, “to flee”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *běda, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeydʰ-, whence English bide, faith and fidelity.

parole.significato: without, aside from, except, minus, free of/from (signifying absence)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bez (“without”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeǵʰs (<+ *h₁éǵʰs (“out”), whence also из (iz)). Cognate with Lithuanian bè (“without; besides”), Latvian bez (“without”), Old Prussian bhe (“without”), Sanskrit बहिस् (bahís, “outside”), Persian بی (bi, “without”). Compare typ
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *biti, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyh₂-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *blějati (“to bleat”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₁- (“to bleat”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bobъ, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰabʰ-.
Inherited from Old East Slavic бобръ (bobrŭ), from Proto-Slavic *bobrъ, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰébʰrus.

parole.significato: elder (a shrub of the genus Sambucus)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bъzъ, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂ǵos (“birch”). Cognate with Bulgarian бъз (băz), Serbo-Croatian базга/bazga, Slovak baza.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bojь, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰoyh₂ós, from *bʰeyh₂- (“to strike, hew”). Cognate with бить (bitʹ, “to beat”), with typical Indo-European nominal o-ablaut.

parole.significato: to wander, to roam, to ramble
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic бродити (broditi), from Proto-Slavic *brodìti, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrodʰ-eye-, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰredʰ-.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bugrъ. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewgʰ- (“to bend”). Cognates include Ukrainian бугі́р (buhír), Lithuanian baũgurs. Non-Slavic cognates include Sanskrit भुग्न (bhugna, “curved, crooked”), Latin fugio (“to flee, to hasten”), English bow.

PIE word  *h₁en Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁énder. Proto-Slavic *vъ(n) Old East Slavic въ (vŭ) Russian в Inherited from Old East Slavic въ (vŭ), from Proto-Slavic *vъ(n), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁n̥, zero-grade form of *h₁én.

parole.significato: added to verbs, forms verbs with the approximate meaning 'in' or 'into'
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic въ- (vŭ-), from Proto-Slavic *vъ(n)-, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁én. The /n/ persists in внять (vnjatʹ). See also в (v), Old East Slavic въ (vŭ), Proto-Slavic *vъ(n). Compare the similar development in с- (s-) from Proto-Slavic *sъ(n)-.

parole.significato: your, yours (2nd-person singular formal or 2nd-person plural)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic вашь (vašĭ), from Proto-Slavic *vašь, from Proto-Indo-European *wōsyo-.

parole.significato: to know (be certain or sure about something or aware of a fact)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *věděti, from Proto-Indo-European *wóyde (“to know”), perfect of *weyd- (“to see, to know”). Cognates include Polish wiedzieć, German wissen, Luxembourgish wëssen and English wit.

Inherited from Old East Slavic вѣдро (vědro), from Proto-Slavic *vědro (“water bucket”), from Proto-Indo-European *wódr̥ (“water”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *wed- (“wet”). Akin to Old Armenian գետ (get, “river”).

parole.significato: to convey, to carry (by vehicle), to deliver, to transport
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *vezti, from Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ-. Cognate with Latin vehō, Sanskrit वहति (vahati), Old English wegan (English weigh). (to be lucky): Compare typologically Latin fortūna (akin to ferō).

Inherited from Old East Slavic вѣникъ (věnikŭ), from Proto-Slavic *věnikъ, from *věnъ (“wreath”) + *-ikъ, details of further origin unclear (possibly from Proto-Indo-European *woh₁y-nos or derived later) but ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *weh₁y- (“to twist, wind, weave”). Cognate to вен (ven),

Inherited from Old East Slavic вѣнъкъ (věnŭkŭ), from Proto-Slavic *věnъkъ, from *věnъ (“wreath”) + *-ъkъ, details of further origin unclear (possibly from Proto-Indo-European *wóh₁y-nós or derived later) but ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *weh₁y- (“to twist, wind, weave”). Cognate to вен (ven),

parole.significato: top, upper part, roof, dome, height
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *vьrxъ (whence also Old Church Slavonic врьхъ (vrĭxŭ)), from Proto-Indo-European *wers-. Balto-Slavic cognates include Lithuanian viršus and Latvian virsus. Other Indo-European cognates include Latin verruca (“a steep place, height”), Ancient Greek ἕρμα (hérma, “reef, roc

Inherited from Old East Slavic вьрвь (vĭrvĭ) + -ка (-ka), from Proto-Slavic *vьrvь (deverbal of *verti), from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to tie, string; rope”) which is ultimately cognate with *wer- (“to turn, bend”) whence the two meanings of the verb. Compare Belarusian вяроўка (vjarówka), Ukrain

parole.significato: branch, bough, limb (woody part of a tree arising from the trunk and usually dividing)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic вѣтвь (větvĭ), from Proto-Slavic *větvь, *větь, from Proto-Indo-European *wéh₁itis. Cognates include Bulgarian ве́тва (vétva), ве́тка (vétka), ве́я (véja), and ве́йка (véjka), Slovene vȇja (tonal orthography), Czech větev, Slovak vetva, Ukrainian ві́та (víta). Non-Slav

From ви́деть (vídetʹ) + -ение (-enije), from Proto-Slavic *viděti (“to see”), from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- (“to know; to see”). Cognate with Lithuanian veidas (“face”), Latvian veids (“form, shape”), Sanskrit वेद (veda, “knowledge”), Avestan 𐬬𐬀𐬉𐬛𐬀𐬵- (vaēdah-, “possession”), Latin videō (“to see”)
Inherited from Old East Slavic воинъ (voinŭ), from Proto-Slavic *vojinъ, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *weyh₁-.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *vorxъ. Cognate with Ukrainian во́рох (vórox, “heap, pile”), also воро́ха (voróxa), Belarusian во́рох (vórox, “noise”), Bulgarian врах (vrah, “sheaves intended for threshing”), Polish zawroch (“blizzard, whirlwind”). More distantly cognate with Russian Church Slavonic врѣ

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *vьrati, 1sg. *vьrǫ (as a verb, only preserved in Russian and Serbo-Croatian). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *werh₁- (“to speak”). Cognate with Serbo-Croatian varati (“to betray”).

From Old East Slavic вꙑ (vy), from Proto-Slavic *vy, from Proto-Indo-European *yúHs. Cognate with Sanskrit यूयम् (yūyam) and English you. Use of Вы as a formal singular is attested in East Slavic literature from the 11th-16th century, under influence of Byzantine speech. It started becoming widespre

parole.significato: out, out from (describing an action of moving outside from inside)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic вꙑ- (vy-), from Proto-Slavic *vy- (“out”), from Proto-Indo-European *úd, or Proto-Indo-European *(H)ud (Derksen), or *ūd- : *ūt- (Černyx). In Slavic, the final consonant was dropped. Cognates include English out, German aus (“out”).
From Old East Slavic вымѧ (vymę), from Proto-Slavic *vymę, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ówHdʰr̥.
Inherited from Old East Slavic гаснꙋти (gasnuti), from Proto-Slavic *gàsnǫti, perfective of *gasìti, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)gʷes-.
Inherited from Old East Slavic глазъ (glazŭ, “ball, eye”), from Proto-Slavic *glazъ (“ball”), from Proto-Indo-European *g(ʰ)el- (“round, spherical, stone”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *glǫbь, from Proto-Indo-European *glewbʰ-, whence English cleave, cleft and glyph.

parole.significato: to oppress, to weigh down, to press
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *gnestì, from Proto-Indo-European *gnet- (“to press together”), from *gen- (“to compress”). Cognate to English knead.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *govoriti, from Proto-Indo-European *gewH- (“to call, cry”) with a *-b⁽ʰ⁾- enlargement, perhaps connected to the synonymous *ǵʰewH-. Cognate to Polish gaworzyć, Czech hovořit, Ukrainian говорити (hovoryty), Serbo-Croatian гово̀рити, Persian گفتن (goftan, “to say, to speak

parole.significato: domestic bovine animals, cattle (cows, oxen, bulls)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *govędo, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷew-n̥d-, from *gʷṓws.

parole.significato: fit, suitable, well-suited, good for, valid, appropriate
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic годьныи (godĭnyi), from Proto-Slavic *godьnъ, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰedʰ- (“to unite, be associated, suit”). Cognate with English good.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *golъ, from Proto-Indo-European *gelH- (“naked, bald”), whence English callow. Compare Polish goły and German kahl.

Inherited from Old East Slavic гонъ (gonŭ), from Proto-Slavic *gonъ, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰónos (compare Ancient Greek φόνος (phónos, “murder”)), o-grade of Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰen- (whence Proto-Slavic *gъnàti, 1sg. *ženǫ, whence Russian гнать (gnatʹ)).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *gaňati, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰen- (“to kill”). Cognate with Albanian gjan (“to hunt”), Lithuanian giñti, Old Norse gunnr (“fight”), Latin dēfendō, Ancient Greek θείνω (theínō), Armenian գան (gan, “beating, blows”).

From Old East Slavic градъ (gradŭ), from Proto-Slavic *gradъ. Cognate with Lithuanian gruodas (Proto-Balto-Slavic *grōda-), Latin grandō, Old Armenian կարկուտ (karkut), Sanskrit ह्रादुनि (hrādúni, “hail”) and possibly with English grind.

parole.significato: to heat (to cause an increase in temperature of an object or space)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *grěti, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰer- (“warm”). Cognate with Ancient Greek θερμός (thermós, “warm”) (whence те́рмос (térmos), термо- (termo-)), Latin formus, furnus, and possibly Proto-Germanic *warmaz (whence English warm).
Inherited from Old East Slavic грѫдь (grǫdĭ), from Proto-Slavic *grǫdь, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰrendʰ-.

From the present participle гряду́щий (grjadúščij, “approaching”), from грясти́ (grjastí, “to be coming, to be approaching”) (грядёт (grjadjót)), from Old East Slavic грѧсти (gręsti), from Proto-Slavic *gręsti (“to go”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrHdʰ-. Cognate with Latin gradior, Gothic 𐌲𐍂𐌹𐌳 (gri
Inherited from Old East Slavic давити (daviti), from Proto-Slavic *dāvìti, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰew-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *děva. Via Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁(y)- cognate with де́ти (déti), дитя́ (ditjá), дои́ть (doítʹ)) Latin fēmina, fētus, fīlius, and many more.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *děvati. By surface analysis, деть (detʹ) + -ва́ть (-vátʹ). Ultimately, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-, whence English do.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *děverь, from Proto-Indo-European *dayh₂wḗr. Cognate with Lithuanian dieveris, Sanskrit देवृ (devṛ́), Armenian տեգր (tegr), Hindi देवर (devar).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *děža, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰoyǵʰyeh₂, from *dʰeyǵʰ- (“to knead (clay)”).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dělo, from Proto-Slavic *děti, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-, whence English do, deed, deem, doom, and via Latin, fact and affair. Other cognates include, via Ancient Greek, English theme, thesis, Sanskrit दधाति (dadhāti, “to put”) Sanskrit धातृ (dhātṛ, “creator”) and
Inherited from Old East Slavic дерево (derevo), from Proto-Slavic *dervo, from Proto-Indo-European *dóru, whence English tree. Doublet of дре́во (drévo).
Inherited from Middle Russian дѧсна́ (djasná), from Proto-Slavic *dęsna, probably ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃dónts.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *děti, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-, whence English do.

parole.significato: child, baby, kid (also used ironically or in similes)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic дѣтѧ (dětę), from Proto-Slavic *dětę. The и of the first syllable in the singular is from дити́на (ditína), nowadays written дети́на (detína) by analogy with the accented де́ти (déti), with regular distant assimilation ѣ…и́ > и…и́. An alternative formulation by Šakhmat
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *do, from Proto-Indo-European *de, whence English to.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dьlgъ, from Proto-Indo-European *dl̥h₁gʰós. Cognate with Sanskrit दीर्घ (dīrgha, “"long"”), Latin longus, English long.

parole.significato: to doze, to slumber, to drowse
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *drěmati, from Proto-Indo-European *drēm-ye-ti, from *drem- (“to sleep”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *drobiti.

From Proto-Slavic *dropъty, whose first part is probably from Proto-Indo-European *dreh₂- (“run”) and the other from Proto-Slavic *pъta (“bird”), which is probably based on Proto-Indo-European *put- (“a young, a child, a little animal”).  Compare Czech drop, Polish drop. Cognate with German Trappe.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ešče (“still, yet”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁esk(ʷ)e(h₁). Cognate with Belarusian яшчэ (jašče), Ukrainian ще (šče), Polish jeszcze.

parole.significato: to feel sorry, to be sorry, to be sad (about something), to regret
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *želěti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žārъ, perhaps together with жара́ (žará) from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰēr- (“heat”, root noun), from *gʷʰer- (“heat, hot”).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žārā̀, perhaps together with жар (žar) for Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰēr- (“heat”, root noun), from *gʷʰer- (“heat, hot”). Cognate with Hindi गर्म (garm) and Hindi गर्मी (garmī), Albanian zjarr, Old Armenian ջեր (ǰer), Latin fornāx, Old Norse varmr, Old Prussian goro (“hear
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žьvati (“to chew”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵyewh₁-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žьlvъ, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰel-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *želza, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰelǵʰ-. Cognate with Old Armenian գեղձ-ք (gełj-kʻ).
Inherited from Old East Slavic жьрдь (žĭrdĭ), from Proto-Slavic *žьrdь, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰerdʰ-. Cognate with Polish żerdź, Slovak žrď.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žerbьcь, from *žerbę, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷrebʰ-. Cognate with Old Church Slavonic жрѣбѧ (žrěbę), Bulgarian жребе́ц (žrebéc). Compare Ancient Greek βρέφος (bréphos, “baby, foetus”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *živica, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷh₃i-u- (“to live”). Cognate with Old Armenian կիւ (kiw).

Inherited from Old East Slavic жолобъ (žolobŭ), from Proto-Slavic *želbъ, , from Proto-Indo-European *gelbh-, *gelebh-. Cognate with Church Slavic жлѣбъ (žlěbŭ), Ukrainian жо́лоб (žólob), Belarusian жо́лаб (žólab), Bulgarian жлеб (žleb), Serbo-Croatian жлије̑б, ждлије̑б, жле̑б, Slovene žlȇb, Old Cze

From Old East Slavic зобота (zobota), from Proto-Slavic [Term?], possibly from Proto-Indo-European *gab- (“to watch, show”). Cognate with Proto-West Germanic *kapēn (“to watch, to look”), Proto-Germanic *kōpijaną (“to look after, care for”) (whence English keep). Also compare Ukrainian забо́та (zabó
Inherited from Old East Slavic зъвати (zŭvati), from Proto-Slavic *zъvati.
From Proto-Slavic *zelenъ, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰelh₃-; whence English yellow, gold, glow and chlorine.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zьrkadlo, from *zьrěti (whence Old Church Slavonic зьрѣти (zĭrěti, “to look at”)) + a suffix originating in Proto-Indo-European *-tlom. Probably a calque of Latin speculum (whence Proto-West Germanic *spēgl, whence German Spiegel and many others). Compare Kashubian szpéd
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zьrno, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵr̥h₂nóm.
From Old East Slavic зобь (zobĭ), from Proto-Slavic *zobь, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵebʰ- (“jaw, mouth”).

Inherited from Old East Slavic золото (zoloto), from Proto-Slavic *zolto, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰolh₃tom (o-grade), from *ǵʰelh₃- (“green, yellow”). Doublet of зла́то (zláto), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic злато (zlato). Compare Ukrainian золото (zoloto), Belarusian золата (zólata), Bulgari
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zętь, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁-.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *i, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ey, an early locative singular determiner, formed from the root *h₁e-, *h₁o-. Compare Greek εἰ (ei, “if”), Gothic 𐌴𐌹 (ei, “and, so that, be it”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jьgъla. Akin to Russian и́го (ígo). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *yewg-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jьgo, from Proto-Indo-European *yugóm, from Proto-Indo-European *yewg-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jьz, from Proto-Indo-European *eǵʰs, *h₁eǵʰs.

Inherited from Old East Slavic изгои (izgoi). Asynchronically analyzable as из- (iz-) + го́ить (góitʹ), from Proto-Slavic *gojiti (“to heal, feed”), the latter being a causative form of жить (žitʹ), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷeyh₃-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kakati. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kakka-. Compare Serbo-Croatian kakati, kakiti, Italian cacare.

parole.significato: buzzard (any bird from the genus Buteo, or, sensu lato, from the subfamily Buteoninae)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kanjukъ / *kanjakъ, from *kaňa, from Proto-Indo-European *kōnyā or *kan- (“to sing”), whence also Proto-Germanic *hanô (“rooster, cock”), Proto-Germanic *hanjō (“hen”) (whence English hen), Latin cicōnia (“stork”), Latin canō (“to sing”), Welsh canu, Ancient Greek καναχέ
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kara (“punishment”), from Proto-Indo-European *kor-. Cognate with Old Irish caire (“blame, disapproval”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kypě̀ti, from Proto-Indo-European *kwep-, whence English cupidity, covet and hope.

parole.significato: to boil (causative of кипе́ть (kipétʹ) (causative inchoative and causative continuative))
parole.testo: Derived from the same root as кипе́ть (kipétʹ, “to boil”), from Proto-Slavic *kypě̀ti, from Proto-Indo-European *kwep-, whence English covet and hope.
From Proto-Slavic *klakъ (“tuft, clump”), from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“to curl up, form into a ball”), see also Old High German klakka.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kogъtь, from Proto-Indo-European *keg-, *keng- (“peg; hook”). Compare Belarusian ко́каць (kókacʹ), Ukrainian коготь (kohotʹ), кіготь (kihotʹ), когіть (kohitʹ).

Inherited from Old East Slavic колеса (kolesa), plural of коло (kolo), from Proto-Slavic *kolo (oblique: *koles-), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷekʷlom (“circle”), *kʷékʷlos (“circle”) whence English wheel and cycle.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kopyto, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *ḱoph₂ós. For the relation with копа́ть (kopátʹ), compare typologically Ancient Greek ὄρυξ (órux). For the relation with копьё (kopʹjó), compare typologically Ancient Greek ὁπλή (hoplḗ), ὅπλον (hóplon).
Inherited from Old East Slavic кора (kora, “bark”), from Proto-Slavic *kora (“bark”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *korbiti, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kerb-, from *(s)ker- (“to turn”). Likely related to Proto-Slavic *krǫpъ (“concise, compact”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic которꙑи (kotoryi), from Proto-Slavic *kotorъjь, *koterъjь, definite of **kotorъ, **koterъ, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷóteros.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krečetъ, perhaps of imitative Proto-Indo-European origin (see Ancient Greek κρέξ (kréx, “corncrake”)). Compare Ancient Greek κέρκνος (kérknos, “a Hierax or an Alektryon”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krupa, from Proto-Indo-European *krowpeh₂.
Inherited from Old East Slavic къто (kŭto), from Proto-Slavic *kъto, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷós.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lъgati (compare Serbo-Croatian ла̀гати/làgati, Bulgarian лъ́жа (lắža)), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lewgʰ-, whence also English lie, German lügen.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *elbedь, *elbędь, *olbǫdь, from Proto-Indo-European *albʰós (“white”).

parole.significato: to lie (to be in a horizontal position)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ležati, from Proto-Indo-European *legʰ-.
Inherited from Old East Slavic лизати (lizati), from Proto-Slavic *līzàti (“to lick”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyǵʰ- (“to lick”).

parole.significato: to deprive, to rob, to bereave
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lišiti, from Proto-Indo-European *leykʷ-, whence English lend and loan.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lъbъ, from Proto-Indo-European *lubʰo.
From Old East Slavic лони (loni), from Proto-Slavic *olni, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ol-ney.

parole.significato: moose (U.S., Canada), elk (British) (an animal belonging to the Alces genus)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic лось (losĭ), from Proto-Slavic *olsь, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁el- (“deer”), whence English elk.

parole.significato: the inner bark of a tree, bast
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lubъ (“bast”), from Proto-Indo-European *lowbʰ-ó-s, from *lewbʰ- (“to peel, cut off, harm”). Cognate with Lithuanian lùpti (“to peel, to shell”), Latvian luba (“narrow strip of wood”), Latin liber (“book, inner bark of a tree”), Proto-Germanic *laubą (whence English leaf
Inherited from Old East Slavic лучь (lučĭ), from Proto-Slavic *lučь (“ray; torch”), from Proto-Indo-European *lowkis, which is derived from *lewk-.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lysъ. Cognate with Belarusian лысы (lysy), Czech lysý, Polish łysy, Ukrainian лисий (lysyj). Akin to Old Armenian լոյս (loys, “light”). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (whence also луна́ (luná), луч (luč)). Compare typologically Ancient Greek φᾰλᾰκρός (phălăkr

parole.significato: to love, to like, to be fond of, to grow fond of (more intensely than нра́виться (nrávitʹsja))
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ľubiti, from Proto-Indo-European *lewbʰ-, whence English love, Sanskrit लुभ्यति (lubhyati, “to desire”), Sanskrit लोभयति (lobhayati, “to make crazy”) and Latin libet.
Inherited from Old East Slavic любꙑ (ljuby), from Proto-Slavic *ľuby, from Proto-Indo-European *lewbʰ-. Cognates include Sanskrit लोभ (lobha, “desire, cupidity”) and English love.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lędvьje, from Proto-Indo-European *lendʰ- (“loins”). Cognate with Sanskrit रन्ध्र (rándhra, “split, hole”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lьgъkъ, from pre-Slavic *h₁ln̥gʷʰ-u-ko, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lengʷʰ-.
Inherited from Old East Slavic макъ (makŭ, “poppy; poppy seeds; poppy seed”), from Proto-Slavic *makъ (“poppy”), from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂kos.
Inherited from Old East Slavic малъ (malŭ), from Proto-Slavic *malъ, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)mal-, *(s)mel-.
Inherited from Old East Slavic малъ (malŭ), from Proto-Slavic *malъ, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)mal-, *(s)mel-, whence English small.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *maniti (“to deceive”), from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂- (“good, timely”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *matorъ, from Proto-Indo-European root *meh₂- (“to ripen, to mature”). Cognate with Serbo-Croatian матор and Latin maturus.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *męzdra, from Proto-Indo-European *mḗms (“flesh, meat”). Cognates include Ukrainian міздря́ (mizdrjá), Belarusian мяздра́ (mjazdrá), Polish miazdra and Czech mázdra as well as Latin membrum. Related to мя́со (mjáso, “meat”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic [Term?], from Proto-Indo-European *mer- (“to shimmer, glisten”).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic [Term?], from Proto-Indo-European *mer- (“to shimmer, glisten”). Cognates include Lithuanian mérkti (“to blink, twinkle”), Ancient Greek μέρα (méra, “morning”), Gothic 𐌼𐌰𐌿𐍂𐌲𐌹𐌽𐍃 (maurgins, “morning”), English morrow.
Inherited from Old East Slavic мѣсѧць (měsęcĭ), from Proto-Slavic *měsęcь, from Proto-Indo-European *mḗh₁n̥s.

parole.significato: to throw, to cast, to toss
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic метати (metati), from Proto-Slavic *metàti (“to throw”), from Proto-Indo-European *met-.
From Old East Slavic метати (metati), from Proto-Slavic *metàti (“to throw”), from Proto-Indo-European *met-.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mětiti, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *méh₁tis (“measure”), from *meh₁-. Akin to Latin mētior (“to measure”), Ancient Greek μῆτις (mêtis, “counsel, plan”), Sanskrit माति (māti, “measure”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *moldъ, from Proto-Indo-European *ml̥dus (“soft, weak”), whence English mild, melt and mollify. Doublet of младо́й (mladój), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic.

parole.significato: large hammer (e.g. a smith's forging hammer), mallet
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *moltъ, from Proto-Indo-European *molh₂-to-, from *melh₂-. Doublet of млат (mlat), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic. Cognate with Latin malleus. Compare typologically кий (kij), кия́нка (kijánka), кува́лда (kuválda) (<< Proto-Indo-European *kewh₂-).

PIE word  *móri Inherited from Old East Slavic море (more), from Proto-Slavic *moře, from Proto-Indo-European *móri, whence English mer- and marsh and through Latin marine, maritime. The astronomical sense is a calque of New Latin mare (“sea”), with which it is cognate.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *morьskъ. By surface analysis, мо́ре (móre) + -ско́й (-skój), from Proto-Slavic *moře, from Proto-Indo-European *móri, whence English marine and maritime.

parole.significato: seaman, sailor, mariner (a member of the crew of a vessel; a person experienced in nautical matters)
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *mořakъ (by surface analysis, мо́ре (móre, “sea”) + -я́к (-ják)), from Proto-Slavic *moře, from Proto-Indo-European *móri, whence English marine and maritime.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mъxъ. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *músos.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *moťi, from Proto-Indo-European *megʰ-. Cognate to Ancient Greek μῆχος (mêkhos, “means, remedy”) and Proto-Germanic *maganą (“to be able, may”) (whence English may, might).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *moťь, from Proto-Indo-European *mógʰtis, *megʰ- (“to allow, be able, help”). Cognate to Proto-Germanic *mahtiz and its descendants like English might. Doublet of мощь (moščʹ), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mošьna, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *mak- (“small (leather) bag or pouch”), see also Lithuanian mãkas, Old High German maga, German Magen (“stomach”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic мѫжь (mǫžĭ), from Proto-Slavic *mǫžь, from Proto-Indo-European *mon-, whence English man.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *morvьjь, from Proto-Indo-European *morwi-.

From Proto-Slavic *mỳšь (“mouse”) (referring to the mouse-like appearance of a flexing muscle), from Proto-Indo-European *muh₂s. For semantic development, compare to Latin mūsculus (“muscle”, literally “little mouse”) and Ancient Greek μῦς (mûs, “mouse; muscle”).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *męso, from Proto-Indo-European *mḗms. Compare Serbo-Croatian meso, Czech maso, Polish mięso, and Slovene meso. Compare Old Prussian mensa (“meat”). Sense 5 refers to the football club being supported by a meat factory in Moscow during the 1930s.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mьrtvъ, from Proto-Indo-European *mr̥twós, *mr̥tós, ultimately from the root *mer- (“to die”), whence also English murder, mortal, morbid and French mourir.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nagъ, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *nogʷós (“naked”); see there for the cognates.

parole.significato: to begin, to start, to commence
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic начѧти (načęti), from Proto-Slavic *načęti. By surface analysis, на- (na-) + -чать (-čatʹ), from Proto-Indo-European *ken- (“new, fresh”), whence English recent and ceno-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *netopyřь, a compound which first part nekto- (e-grade) is cognate to Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts (o-grade).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nizъ, from Proto-Indo-European *nei-ǵʰ-? (Derksen) or *ni- (“down”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nizъkъ, from Proto-Indo-European *ni-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nъ, from Proto-Indo-European *nu. Cognate with English now and Latin num ("now") and nunc (< *num + ce, "now").
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nogъtь, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃nogʰ-, *h₃nogʷʰ-.
Inherited from Old East Slavic нꙑнѣ (nyně), from Proto-Slavic *nyně, from Proto-Indo-European *nu (“now”), compare with Ukrainian ни́ні (nýni), German nun, English now.
Derived from Old East Slavic нꙑнѣ (nyně) (whence ны́не (nýne)), from Proto-Slavic *nyně, from Proto-Indo-European *nu (“now”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nyrnǫti, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁én. Compare Old Church Slavonic нирıати (nirıati), Belarusian ны́рка (nýrka), Bulgarian ни́рна (nírna).

From Proto-Slavic *ňaňa, a reduplicated nursery formation. Similar nursery formations are widespread in Proto-Indo-European; compare Sanskrit नना (nanā́, “mother”), Ancient Greek νάννα (nánna, “aunt”), Albanian nënë (“mother”), Welsh nain (“grandmother”). The related form ня́нька (njánʹka) was first
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *o(b), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ebʰi.
Inherited from Old East Slavic оба (oba), from Proto-Slavic *oba, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰóh₁, whence also Lithuanian abù, Latvian abi, Latin ambo, Ancient Greek ἄμφω (ámphō).
Inherited from Old East Slavic око (oko), from Proto-Slavic *oko, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ekʷ-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *olьxa, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élis-. Compare Serbo-Croatian јо́ха, jóha.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *osa, from Proto-Indo-European *wobʰseh₂.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *osьla or *osla̋, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ-l-. Cognate with Old Church Slavonic осла (osla), Slovak osla, Slovene ósla, Polish osełka. More distant cognates include Armenian ասեղ (aseġ, “needle”) and dialectal German Achel (“awn”).

Inherited from Old East Slavic осень (osenĭ), from Proto-Slavic *esenь, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁es-en-, whence English earn and German Ernte (“harvest”). Doublet of есень (jesenʹ) and есеня (jesenja), cognate with Belarusian во́сень (vósjenʹ) and Ukrainian о́сінь (ósinʹ).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *opsina, *opsa, from Proto-Indo-European *(H)osp-eh₂, from *(H)osp-. Cognates include Ukrainian оси́на (osýna), Belarusian асі́на (asína), Lithuanian ẽpušė, Latvian apse, Old Prussian abse and Proto-Germanic *aspō.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ostrъ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱrós.
Inherited from Old East Slavic отьць (otĭcĭ), from Proto-Slavic *otьcь, from Proto-Indo-European *átta.

parole.significato: to graze, to pasture, to shepherd
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *pastì, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂-.

parole.significato: to fart (noisily, as opposed to бздеть)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *pьrděti, from Proto-Indo-European *perd-. Cognate to English fart, French péter.

Inherited from Old East Slavic передъ (peredŭ), from Proto-Slavic *perdъ, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *per-, whence also пере- (pere-), перез (perez). Doublet of пред (pred), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic.

parole.significato: to move, to trudge, to drag the feet
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *perti, from Proto-Indo-European *préy, whence English fare and ferry as well as German fahren.
From пере- (pere-) + че́сть (čéstʹ), from Proto-Slavic *čьstь, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kʷit-tis.
пере- (pere-) + че́сть (čéstʹ), from Proto-Slavic *čьstь, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kʷit-tis.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *pьrsь, from Proto-Indo-European, cognate with Serbo-Croatian пр̏са/pȑsa (“breast”), Slovak prs, prsia (“bosom”).
From Late Proto-Slavic *pěti, from Proto-Indo-European *poiH-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *pěxъ, *pěxota, which is derived from Proto-Indo-European *pēd-, a variant of *ped-. Cognate to Russian под (pod, “floor, ground”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *pěšь. Ultimately a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *pṓds.
Inherited from Old East Slavic пиво (pivo, “drink, beverage; beer”), from Proto-Slavic *pivo (“drink, beverage; beer”), from Proto-Indo-European *ph₃iwom.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *pitati, from Proto-Indo-European *peyt- (“food, nutrition”). Cognate with Old Church Slavonic питѣти (pitěti) and Serbo-Croatian pȉtati.
Inherited from Old East Slavic пити (piti), from Proto-Slavic *piti (“to drink”), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₃- (“to drink”). Related to Latin pōtāre (“to drink”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *plavati, from Proto-Indo-European *plew-. Cognate with English float.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *plodъ, from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₁-, whence English full, plenty and poly-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ploskъ. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂- (“thin, flat”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *plъ̃tъ, from Proto-Indo-European *plew-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *poľe, from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *poltьno, from Proto-Indo-European *polto- (“cloth”), from Proto-Indo-European *pel-. Doublet of платно́ (platnó), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic.

Inherited from Old East Slavic полъ (polŭ, “open from above, uncovered”), attested in a 14th-c. birchbark letter (No. 59) in "полои води" 'floodwaters.GEN.SG' (cf. Russian половодье (polovodʹje)). Modern meaning attested since 1636. Related to Proto-Slavic *poľe (“field”) and *polnъ (“flat, smooth,
From the verb постоя́ть (postojátʹ), from по- (po-) + стоя́ть (stojátʹ), from Proto-Slavic *stojati (“to stand”), from Proto-Indo-European *stoh₂-.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *potolъkъ, from *tьlo (“ground, bottom”), from Proto-Indo-European *telh₂-o- (“ground”), from *telh₂- (“to bear, carry”). Cognates include Sanskrit तल (tala, “surface, bottom”), Latin tellūs (“ground, land”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic приꙗзнь (prijaznĭ), from Proto-Slavic *prijàznь, from Proto-Indo-European *priH- (“to love”).

parole.significato: to jump, to spring, to leap
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *prygati, from Proto-Indo-European *prew- (“to jump”). Cognates include Sanskrit प्रवते (pravate, “to jump”), Persian پریدن, English frolic, and German fröhlich.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *pъtakъ, derived from *pъta, from Proto-Indo-European *peth₂- (“to fly”).

Inherited from Old East Slavic пьшеница (pĭšenica), from Proto-Slavic *pьšenica. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peys-, whence also пиха́ть (pixátʹ). Compare typologically Latin trīticum (< trītus, p.p.p of terō), Latin secāle (<? Proto-Indo-European *sek-).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *radǫga. The first element more likely derives from Proto-Slavic *radъ (“glad, dear, willing”) than folk etymology’s Proto-Slavic *rajь. Compare Russian весёлка (vesjólka, “rainbow”) (dialectal) related to весёлый (vesjólyj, “merry, cheerful, happy, convivial, gleeful, li

parole.significato: sallow, willow (Salix fragilis, Salix caprea) (tree or wood)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *orkyta, which Pokorny connects to Ancient Greek ἄρκευθος (árkeuthos, “juniper”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *h₂erkʷ- (“bend”). Also compare Latvian ērkšķis (“thorn bush”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ordlo, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂érh₃trom.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *orsti, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃er-.

Inherited from Old East Slavic рѣшити (rěšiti, “to untie, absolve”), from Proto-Slavic *rěšiti, from Proto-Indo-European *wreyḱ- (“to twist, bend”). Cognates include Ukrainian ріши́ти (rišýty), Belarusian рашы́ць (rašýcʹ), Serbo-Croatian решити, Czech řešit.
Inherited Old East Slavic ръзати (rŭzati), from Proto-Slavic *rъzati, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *rewǵ-. Cognate with Czech ržát.

parole.significato: shy, timid, bashful (lacking in courage or confidence)
parole.testo: From Old East Slavic робъ (robŭ, “serf”) + -кий (-kij), from Proto-Slavic *orbъ (“slave”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃órbʰos (“orphan”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic румꙗнъ (rumjanŭ), from Proto-Slavic *ruměnъ, from earlier *rudměnъ, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rewdʰ-.

parole.significato: fair(-haired), blond(e), light brown (of hair), dirty blond
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic русъ (rusŭ), from Proto-Slavic *rusъ, from earlier *rudsъ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rowdʰ-s-o-.
Inherited from Old East Slavic рꙑжии (ryžii), from Proto-Slavic *ryďь, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rūdʰ-yo-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ryti, from Proto-Slavic *rūti. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(H)rewH-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rębъ (“speckled, spotted”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁erbʰ-, see also Ancient Greek ὀρφνός (orphnós, “dark brown”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *svãrъ, from the Proto-Indo-European root *swer- (“to resound, enunciate, pronounce; to swear”). Cognate with Old Norse swara (“answer”), English answer, swear.

parole.significato: holy, sacred (dedicated to a religious purpose)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic свѧтъ (svętŭ), from Proto-Slavic *svętъ, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱwen- (“holy”).

parole.significato: the father of one's husband; father-in-law
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic свекръ (svekrŭ), from Proto-Slavic *svekrъ, from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱuros.
Inherited from Old East Slavic село (selo), from Proto-Slavic *selo, from Proto-Indo-European *sel-.
PIE word  *septḿ̥ Inherited from Old East Slavic семь (semĭ), седмь (sedmĭ), from Proto-Slavic *sedmь, from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥.

Inherited from Middle Russian сѣчень (sěčenʹ), from Proto-Slavic *sěčьňь. Inherited from Proto-Slavic *sěťi, from Proto-Indo-European *sek- (“to cut”). Cognates include Ukrainian сі́чень (síčenʹ, “January”), Polish styczeń, Serbo-Croatian siječanj, and Macedonian сечко (sečko, “February”). Related t

From ска́ред (skáred) + -ный (-nyj), from Proto-Slavic *skarędъ. Cognates include Old Church Slavonic скарѧдь (skarędĭ), Czech škaredý and Polish szkaradny. Vasmer also suspects relation with Sanskrit अवस्कर (avaskara, “trash, ordure”), Ancient Greek σκῶρ (skôr, “dung”), and Proto-Germanic *skarną (
Inherited from Proto-Slavic [Term?], from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kel-.
Inherited from Old East Slavic слухъ (sluxŭ), Proto-Slavic *sluxъ, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱlew-, whence Sanskrit श्रुति (śruti), English listen, and loud.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *slušati, from an earlier *sluxěti, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱlew-, whence English listen and Sanskrit श्रोषति (śroṣati, “to listen, obey”).

parole.significato: to pass (for), to have the reputation (for), to be said / reputed
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *slyti, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱlew- (“to hear”). Compare Ancient Greek κλύω (klúō, “to hear, listen”), κλυτός (klutós, “famous”), Latin inclitus (“renowned”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *slỳšati, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱlew-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *slina, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂leyH- (“to smear”). Cognates include Old Church Slavonic слина (slina), Bulgarian слю́на (sljúna), Czech slina, Polish ślina.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *snъxa, from Proto-Indo-European *snusós.

Inherited from Old East Slavic соловии (solovii), from Proto-Slavic *solvьjь, from *solvъ (“cream-colored”) + *-ьjь, from Proto-Indo-European *saluo-. Compare typologically ря́бчик (rjábčik) (akin to рябо́й (rjabój)), сиза́рь (sizárʹ) (akin to си́зый (sízyj), also note го́лубь (gólubʹ) (akin to голу
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *solma, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱolh₂mos.

PIE word  *sḗh₂l Inherited from Proto-Slavic *solь, from Proto-Indo-European *séh₂l-, *sḗh₂l. Cognates include Sanskrit सलिल (salila), Ancient Greek ἅλς (háls), Armenian աղ (aġ), Latin sāl, and Old English sealt (English salt).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *sъ̀nъ, from Proto-Indo-European *supnós (whence also гипно́з (gipnóz)).
An assimilation of сцать (scatʹ), from Proto-Slavic *sьcati (“to piss”) < *sьkati, from Proto-Indo-European *sikʷ-.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *sъsora; compare Old Church Slavonic сваръ (svarŭ, “quarrel”). Ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *swer-; further related to English swear via Proto-Germanic *swarō.

parole.significato: to whip, to lash, to flog
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *stegati, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)teyg-. Cognate with English stick and Ancient Greek στίγμα (stígma), among others.

parole.significato: to spread, to lay, to make (bed)
parole.testo: See Proto-Slavic *stьlati (“to spread”), from Proto-Indo-European *stel- / *stl-. Compare Polish ścielić.

parole.significato: to spread, to lay, to make (bed)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *stьlati (“to spread”), from Proto-Indo-European *stel- / *stl-.

parole.significato: stand (a device to hold something upright or aloft)
parole.testo: From the verb стоя́ть (stojátʹ), from Proto-Slavic *stojati (“to stand”), from Proto-Indo-European *stoh₂-.
Inherited from Old East Slavic стоꙗти (stojati), from Proto-Slavic *stojati (“to stand”), from Proto-Indo-European *stoh₂-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *strěla, from Proto-Indo-European *strel-, *strēl-, from *ster- (“line, streak, stripe; jet, spurt; beam”).

parole.significato: to cut (hair, fur, grass, etc.), to shear, to clip, to trim
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic стричи (striči), from Proto-Slavic *striťi, from Proto-Indo-European *streyg-.

Inherited from Old East Slavic ступити (stupiti), from Proto-Slavic *stǫpiti, from Proto-Indo-European *stab- (“to support”). Compare Upper Sorbian stupić, Polish stąpić, Czech stoupit, Serbo-Croatian stupiti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *sǫdì, from Proto-Indo-European *som-dʰh₁-ih₂, from *som- + *dʰeh₁- + *-ih₂.
Inherited from Old East Slavic сука (suka), from Proto-Slavic *sùka, further etymology unclear. Possibly from Proto-Indo-European *ḱwṓ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *sьcati (“to piss”) < *sьkati, from Proto-Indo-European *sikʷ-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *sytъ (“satiated, full”), from Proto-Indo-European *s(e)h₂tos, from *seh₂- (“to satiate”).

parole.significato: to slurp (drink or eat (liquid food) noisily)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *sьrbati, from Proto-Indo-European *srebʰ-. Cognate with English slurp.

parole.significato: to hide, to conceal; to harbour (a feeling)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tajìti, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)teh₂y-.

parole.significato: net used for trapping rabbits or other animals
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic тенето (teneto), тонето (toneto), from Proto-Slavic *teneto, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ten-. Cognates include Lithuanian tiñklas, German Dohne, Latin tenus.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tesla / *teslo (“adze”), from Proto-Indo-European *tetḱ-dʰlo-, from *tetḱ-. Cognate with Serbo-Croatian те̏сла, Polish ciosła, Old Norse þexla (“axe”), Old High German dehsala (“axe, adze”).

Inherited from Old East Slavic тѣснъ (těsnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *těsnъ (“narrow”). According to Václav Machek, it is related to Ancient Greek στενός (stenós, “narrow, tight”), thus making both derive from Proto-Indo-European *ténh₂us (“thin”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tъkanь, derived from ткать (tkatʹ, “to weave”), from Proto-Slavic *tъkati, from Proto-Indo-European *trūk-, *trūg- (“to press, beat”).

parole.significato: to weary (with a rather negative intention), to torment, to torture, to languish
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic томити (tomiti), from Proto-Slavic *tomiti, from Proto-Indo-European *temH-. Cognate with Old Church Slavonic томити (tomiti).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tъpati, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewp-. Related to Old Church Slavonic тъпати (tŭpati), Proto-Hellenic *túpt͏̌ō, Latin stupeō.

parole.significato: footfall, tread, tramp, trample, stamp, stomp
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tъpъtъ, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewp- or ultimately, onomatopoeic.

parole.significato: to sharpen, to hone, to whet
parole.testo: Follows from the diachronic convergence of Proto-Slavic *tъčiti (“to point, to sharpen”) from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewk- (“to hew”) and Proto-Slavic *točiti (“to stiffen”) from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tek- (“to rig, to fixate”). Morphologically, an iterative of Russian ткнуть (tknutʹ, “to poke”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic трудъ (trudŭ), from Proto-Slavic *trudъ, from Proto-Indo-European *trewd-, whence also English threat.
Inherited from Old East Slavic тугъ (tugŭ), from Proto-Slavic *tǫgъ (“hard, strong”), from Proto-Indo-European *tengʰ- (extension of Proto-Indo-European *ten-).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tȗrъ, from Proto-Indo-European *táwros.

From Old East Slavic туча (tuča), from Proto-Slavic *tǫča, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tenk- (“to contract”). Compare the Slavic Old Church Slavonic тѫча (tǫča), Ukrainian ту́ча (túča), Polish tęcza and the Non-Slavic Gothic 𐌸𐌴𐌹𐍈𐍉𐌽 (þeiƕōn) and Old Norse þéttr. Unrelated to Russian ту́чный

parole.significato: second-person singular, nominative case: you, thou
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic тꙑ (ty), from Proto-Slavic *ty, from Proto-Indo-European *túh₂. Cognate with Old Church Slavonic тꙑ (ty).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *teplъ, from Proto-Indo-European *tep-.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *uvy, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wai. Cognate with English woe, Latin vae, Lithuanian vai̇̃, Sanskrit उवे (uvé), Hittite [script needed] (uwai), Persian وای (vây).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ǫgъlъ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂engulos (“joint?”), from *h₂eng- (“corner”).

Inherited from Old East Slavic уда (uda), from Proto-Slavic *ǫda, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *and-, *end-. Cognate with Ukrainian ву́дка (vúdka), Belarusian вуда́ (vudá), Church Slavonic ѫда (ǫda), ѫдица (ǫdica), Bulgarian въ́дица (vắdica), Serbo-Croatian у̏дица, Slovene ȯ́dica (tonal orthography), Cze
From Proto-Slavic *umerti, (*u- + *merti) from Proto-Indo-European *mer-.

Inherited from Old East Slavic уродъ (urodŭ, “feebleminded, witless, foolish”), from Proto-Slavic *ǫrodъ, ancient deverbative of *roditi with nominal negative prefix *ǫ-, zero grade of *ne, from Proto-Indo-European *n̥-.

parole.significato: to fall asleep, to go to sleep
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *usъnǫti (“to fall asleep”), from *u- (“away”) + *sъpati (“to sleep”), from Proto-Indo-European *swep-.

parole.significato: to have time, to find time
parole.testo: By surface analysis, у- (u-) + спеть (spetʹ), from Proto-Slavic *spěti, from Proto-Indo-European *spewd- (“press, hurry”), whence English speed.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *usta, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃éh₁os (“mouth”). Cognates include Sanskrit आस् (ās, “mouth”) and Latin ōs (“mouth”). Compare Polish usta.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *uxo, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ṓws. Cognate with Old Armenian ունկն (unkn), Gothic 𐌰𐌿𐍃𐍉 (ausō), Ancient Greek οὖς (oûs), Latin auris, Persian هوش (huš, hôš, “intellect”).

parole.significato: motion, movement, travel, progress, locomotion, headway
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic ходъ (xodŭ), from Proto-Slavic *xodъ, from Proto-Indo-European *sod-, whence Ancient Greek ὁδός (hodós, “threshold; road, path, journey”) and thereby English suffix -ode.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *čadъ (“smoke, fumes”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷēd-o-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *čelo, from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₃os.
Inherited from Old East Slavic чересъ (čeresŭ), from Proto-Slavic *čersъ, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kert-, from *(s)ker-. Doublet of чрез (črez), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic.
By assimilation from Old East Slavic сочевица (sočevica), from сочиво (sočivo, “lentil seed”), from Proto-Slavic *sočivo, probably from *sòkъ (“juice”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sokʷos.
Inherited from Old East Slavic чинъ (činŭ), from Proto-Slavic *činъ, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷey-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *čьstiti, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kʷit-tis. Compare Ukrainian чти́ти (čtýty), Polish czcić.
Inherited from Old East Slavic чьто (čĭto), from Proto-Slavic *čьto, a univerbation of Proto-Indo-European *kʷid and *tód.

parole.significato: chock, block of wood, a small, severed part of a tree
parole.testo: Related to Lithuanian kiáuras, Latvian саũrs, Lithuanian kiùrstu, kiuraũ, kiùrti, skiaurė̃, Middle High German schore. Less likely Polish szczur (“rat”). Inherited from Proto-Slavic *čurъ or *ščurъ from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kew-. The pejorative sense of "Caucasian or Central Asian immigrant", whi

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *čùti, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewh₁- (“to perceive”), whence English show and caution, as well as German schauen (“to look”), thereby English anschauung and weltanschauung (“sense of the world, worldview”).

parole.significato: fur, hair (animal hair or human body hair; contrast волосы and мех)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic сьрсть (sĭrstĭ), (since the 14th century) шьрсть (šĭrstĭ), from Proto-Slavic *sьrstь, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱer(s)- (“rough hair, bristle”) + *-tь, whence also Lithuanian šerys, English hair.
Inherited from Old East Slavic щадѣти (ščaděti, “to keep, spare”), from Proto-Slavic *ščęditi, from Proto-Indo-European *skend-. See also ску́дный (skúdnyj).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ščebьňь, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *skabʰ- (“to scratch”). Related to ско́бель (skóbelʹ, “shaving/drawing knife, spokeshave”), скобли́ть (skoblítʹ, “to scrape, to scrub”), щебло́ (ščebló, “splinter, chip”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ščepa, from *skopiti (“to castrate”), from Proto-Indo-European *skēp-. Cognate with German Schüppe.
Inherited from Old East Slavic ꙗзъ (jazŭ), from Proto-Slavic *(j)azъ, from Proto-Indo-European *éǵh₂. Doublet of эго (ego).

parole.significato: to show (to have someone see something)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic ꙗвити (javiti), from Proto-Slavic *aviti, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ew- (“to perceive, see, be aware of”). Cognate with Proto-Germanic *awiz (“obvious”) and Sanskrit आविस् (āvís, “manifestly, evidently”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *avь (“obvious, apparent, real”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ew- (“apparent”). Cognates include Polish jawa, Ukrainian я́ва (jáva), ява́ (javá) or яв (jav).
Inherited from Old East Slavic агнѧ (agnę), ꙗгнѧ (jagnę) + -ёнок (-jónok), from Proto-Slavic *agnę, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂egʷn-, the stem of *h₂egʷnós. Compare а́гнец (ágnec).
Inherited from Old East Slavic ꙗрьмъ (jarĭmŭ), from Proto-Slavic *arьmo, *arьmъ, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂er-.

parole.significato: to fidget, to squirm, to move restlessly (to twist in discomfort, especially from shame or embarrassment)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jьrzati, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁erǵʰ- (“mount (sexually), cover, copulate”). Cognate to Lithuanian er̃žilas, ar̃žilas (“stallion”), aržùs (“hot-tempered, lustful”), Old Norse argr (“effeminate”), German arg (“bad”), English eerie.
